query: Starting from crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more metals, what single intervention could overcome the unresolved risk of structural or chemical instability during operation in the 773–1173 K catalytic regime? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the mechanism by which it would preserve stability, the predicted outcome relative to the same nanoparticles without the intervention, relevant temperature, time, and compositional boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a thermal-exposure experiment with measurements and failure criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a secondary phase of thermodynamically stable, refractory metal carbides (e.g., TiC, ZrC) or oxides (e.g., Al2O3) via in-situ formation during nanoparticle synthesis will suppress the high-temperature phase decomposition and elemental segregation of near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles in the 773–1173 K regime by pinning grain boundaries and reducing the chemical potential gradient for diffusion.
generation.material_initial_state: Crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles composed of five or more refractory transition metals (e.g., Nb, Mo, Ta, W, V) in a single BCC phase, synthesized via in-situ alloy formation from elemental powders.
generation.intervention: In-situ formation of a dispersed secondary phase of refractory metal carbides (e.g., TiC) or oxides (e.g., Al2O3) comprising 5–10 vol.% during the nanoparticle synthesis process.
generation.conditions: Thermal exposure in an inert or catalytic atmosphere at temperatures between 773 K and 1173 K for durations up to 1000 hours, with a compositional boundary of near-equiatomic ratios (±5%) for the five principal elements.
generation.structural_mediator: Zener pinning of grain boundaries and solute drag effects provided by the dispersed secondary phase particles, which restrict atomic diffusion and inhibit the nucleation of decomposition products (e.g., B2 ordered phases or Laves phases).
generation.mechanism: The high interfacial energy between the secondary phase particles and the matrix creates a thermodynamic barrier to grain growth and phase separation. The particles act as sinks for vacancies and solute atoms, effectively lowering the driving force for the entropy-driven decomposition into ordered phases or the precipitation of brittle intermetallics that typically occur in refractory HEAs at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The composite nanoparticles will retain their single-phase BCC solid-solution structure and high surface area (preventing sintering) after 1000 hours at 1173 K, exhibiting negligible mass loss and no significant phase transformation, whereas the baseline nanoparticles without the secondary phase will undergo significant phase decomposition (e.g., formation of B2 or Laves phases), grain coarsening, and potential elemental segregation.
generation.baseline: Near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles of the same five-metal composition synthesized without the intentional addition of carbide or oxide forming elements (e.g., Ti, Al) or without the in-situ reinforcement step.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds for nanoparticles with a secondary phase volume fraction between 5% and 15%; beyond 15%, the catalytic activity may be blocked, and below 5%, the pinning effect may be insufficient to prevent decomposition at 1173 K. The hypothesis assumes the secondary phase remains thermodynamically stable and does not react with the matrix to form brittle intermetallics.
generation.uncertainty: The specific interaction between the secondary phase and the specific catalytic reactants in the 773–1173 K regime is not fully characterized; there is a risk that the secondary phase could catalyze unwanted side reactions or that the in-situ formation process might lead to non-uniform distribution of the secondary phase in the nanoparticle ensemble.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of near-equiatomic NbMoTaWV nanoparticles: Set A (Baseline) via standard in-situ alloy formation, and Set B (Intervention) via in-situ formation with the addition of Ti and C precursors to generate TiC. Subject both sets to isothermal thermal exposure at 1173 K for 1000 hours in an inert atmosphere. Perform identical catalytic testing (e.g., CO oxidation) on both sets before and after exposure.
measurements: High-resolution Transmission Electron Microscopy (HRTEM) to quantify phase composition and grain size distribution.
X-ray Diffraction (XRD) to detect the emergence of secondary phases (e.g., B2, Laves) or ordered structures.
Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS) of the post-exposure gas stream to measure elemental volatilization or segregation.
Catalytic activity metrics (conversion rate, selectivity) before and after thermal exposure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if Set B (with secondary phase) exhibits a statistically significant increase in the fraction of decomposed phases (e.g., >10% volume fraction of non-BCC phases) or a grain size increase >50% compared to Set A after 1000 hours at 1173 K, or if the catalytic activity of Set B degrades more rapidly than Set A due to secondary phase poisoning or sintering.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

Abstract A novel metal matrix composite based on the NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy (HEA) was designed by the in-situ formation method. The microstructure, phase evolution, and compression mechanical properties at room temperature of the composite are investigated in detail. The results confirmed that the composite was primarily composed of body-centered cubic solid solution with a small amount of titanium carbides and alumina. With the presence of approximately 7.0 vol. % Al 2 O 3 and 32.2 vol. % TiC reinforced particles, the compressive fracture strength of the composite (1542 MPa) was increased by approximately 50% compared with that of the as-cast NbMoCrTiAl HEA. In consideration of the superior oxidation resistance, the P/M NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy composite could be considered as a promising high temperature structural material. Keywords: high entropy alloys, metal matrix composites, mechanical properties

High entropy or multi principal element alloys are a promising and relatively young concept for designing alloys. The idea of creating alloys without a single main alloying element opens up a wide space for possible new alloy compositions. High entropy alloys based on refractory metals such as W, Mo, Ta or Nb are of interest for future high temperature applications e.g., in the aerospace or chemical industry. However, producing refractory metal high entropy alloys by conventional metallurgical methods remains challenging. For this reason, the feasibility of laser-based additive manufacturing of the refractory metal high entropy alloy W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 by laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is investigated in the present work. In-situ alloy formation from mixtures of easily available elemental powders is employed to avoid an expensive atomization of pre-alloyed powder. It is shown that PBF-LB/M of W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 is in general possible and that a complete fusion of the powder mixture without a significant number of undissolved particles is achievable by in-situ alloy formation during PBF-LB/M when selecting favorable process parameter combinations.
